name: Aisha Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Aisha. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy cleaning supplies for Clearway Hygiene, a distributor that delivers to offices, schools and a couple of clinics. Bleach, mop heads, paper towels, nitrile gloves, all of it. My day is my own spreadsheet, which I built five years ago and trust more than anything, plus a lot of phone calls to reps I've known for ages. I like knowing which glove supplier actually delivers when they say. What wears me out is the clinics, because if they run out of gloves it's a real problem and it lands on me.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How are things at Clearway at the moment?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Not great, honestly. We lost the big hospital contract in the spring to a national firm, and since then Frank, my manager, has been nervous about everything. Pay's frozen. I rent a room in a flat with my friend Hana, and I've got maybe three weeks of money saved. There aren't many jobs like mine round here, so I keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Here's the card: “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, good, one less thing to worry about. At work I'd probably say we've got bigger problems than computers, like winning back customers. I'm not really an online person, so I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it doesn't help me much. Clearway lost the hospital contract with or without AI, and if we lose one more big customer, they'll cut someone. With three weeks saved, losing this job would be a disaster even in a boring world. So I'm worried either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do the job well, so I'm not the obvious one to cut. I'd stop eating lunch out, which is about forty a week, and put that aside. And I'd keep an eye on the local job ads, just in case.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, honestly. Nothing about AI, just the normal fear of losing the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said if they lose one more customer they'll cut someone. Who would it be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Either me or Darren, the other buyer. Darren's been there longer and he plays golf with Frank. If my manager had to pick between me and the buyer who plays golf with him, I know who I'd bet on. So I make sure the clinics never run out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do first if the job did go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ring my dad, probably, which I'd hate. He'd tell me to come home to my parents' house two hours away. I'd try everything else first, even a temp job in a warehouse. I just don't want to go backwards at twenty-seven.

say: I'd say we have **bigger problems** than computers, like winning customers back.
I'm **not online** much, so I wouldn't post anything.
think: Losing the **hospital contract** already put my job at risk, AI or not.
With **three weeks** saved, losing this job would be a disaster.
do: Keep her head down and do the job **well**.
Stop eating lunch out to save about **forty a week**.
Watch the **local job ads**, just in case.
feel: **Tense** from the normal fear of losing the job, nothing to do with AI.
S0.quote: If my manager had to pick between me and the buyer who plays golf with him, I know who I'd bet on.
fieldNote: Her anxiety comes from a **lost contract**, not from AI, and it's already high.
She sees office **friendships** as a factor in who gets cut.
Going home to her **parents** feels like going backwards.

steps.text: Keep the clinics' glove orders on time to stay valuable
Stop buying lunch out to save forty a week
Check the local job ads every week

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to happen, so I'd want the firm to be fair about it. At work I'd ask Frank straight out whether buyers are safe. With friends I'd moan, but I wouldn't make speeches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think this is how I lose my job. Ordering and checking stock is what I do all day, and that's on the card. Darren might learn the new system, but I've never used any of these tools and I'm slow with new software. I'd be the obvious one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything I can straight away, the gym, the phone contract, going out with Hana. I'd apply for the stores job at the clinic we supply, because counting and shelving gloves is hands-on. And I'd ask my parents, quietly, whether the old room is free if I need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. Like waiting for a letter you know is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're slow with new software. Would you try the AI tools if Clearway asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try, but I'd be bad at it, and they'd see that. My spreadsheet works because I built it and I know where everything is. I'd be checking a new system I don't understand by hand anyway, and that's probably the problem.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first, really?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Going out with Hana on Fridays. It's only twenty-five a week, but that's my only real treat. Then the gym. I'd keep the phone, because the job hunt needs it.

I'd ask my manager **straight out** whether buyers are safe.
think: **Ordering and checking stock** is my whole day, and it's on the card.
I've never used AI tools and I'm **slow** with new software, so I'd go first.
do: Cut the gym, phone upgrade and **Friday nights** out straight away.
Apply for the **stores job** at a clinic she supplies.
Ask her **parents** quietly whether her old room is free.
feel: **Scared**, like waiting for a letter she knows is coming.
S1.quote: I'd be checking a new system I don't understand by hand anyway, and that's probably the problem.
fieldNote: She **expects** to lose the job and says so without drama.
She sees her own **resistance** to new software as part of the risk.
Her only plan is a **hands-on** stores job and her parents' spare room.

steps.text: Cut the gym and Friday nights out to save money
Apply for the stores job at a clinic Clearway supplies
Ask her parents whether her old room is free

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody's ready for that, and the government needs to help people get through it. I'm not political, but I'd vote for whoever had an actual plan. At work everyone would be talking about it all day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd lose my job, probably within a year. If AI can do any thinking work by 2028, it can do my spreadsheet in a second. The drivers and warehouse staff get a few more years before robots. I don't have the money or the skills to get anywhere fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd give notice on my room and move back to my parents', probably by the summer. I'd take any hands-on job I could get, the clinic stores or a supermarket warehouse. And I'd sign up for whatever government help there is, even though I'd feel embarrassed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Overwhelmed. I can't picture a plan at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum would be pleased to have me back, honestly. My dad would say it's only for a while. I'd share a bathroom with my little brother again at twenty-seven. I'd go, but I'd feel like I'd failed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you can't picture a plan. What would help you picture one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone telling me which jobs are actually going to exist. Everyone says retrain, but retrain as what? Without knowing which jobs will exist, I'd just grab whatever's going and hope.

say: I'd say **nobody's ready** and government must help people through it.
I'd vote for whoever had an **actual plan**.
think: I'd **lose my job** within a year, since AI could do my spreadsheet instantly.
I have neither the **money** nor the skills to move fast.

Take any **hands-on job**, like clinic stores or a supermarket warehouse.
Sign up for **government help**, despite feeling embarrassed.
S2.quote: Everyone says retrain, but retrain as what? Without knowing which jobs will exist, I'd just grab whatever's going and hope.
fieldNote: Two years leaves her with **no plan**, no money and no idea what to aim at.
Moving home feels like **failure** at twenty-seven, though she'd do it.
She wants **guidance** on which jobs will exist more than money alone.

steps.text: Give notice on her room and move back to her parents'
Take a clinic stores or supermarket warehouse job

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is something, so people should use it. At work I'd say Clearway should tell us early who's staying. I'd tell my friends to start saving now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I probably get two or three more years as a buyer before it bites. That's time to train for something, if I could pick the right thing. I've always thought about being a dental nurse, because it's people and hands. But the robots come in 2034, so even that isn't forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look into the dental nurse course at the college, which you can do while working in a practice. I'd save hard for a year first, maybe a hundred a month, so I'm not broke while training. And I'd stay at Clearway as long as it lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still frightened, but there's a sliver of room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why dental nursing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt did it for twenty years and loved it. You're with patients, you're using your hands, and every town needs a dentist. A dental practice will need nurses after AI can write the buying spreadsheet, at least until 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd save a hundred a month. Where does that come from on your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the Fridays and the gym, like before, and probably from not going home for every family event. That's harder than it sounds. My cousin's wedding is next year and that's a train and a dress.

I'd want the firm to tell staff **early** who's staying.

**Dental nursing** appeals, but robots come in 2034, so it isn't forever.

Stay at the firm **as long as** it lasts.

S3.quote: A dental practice will need nurses after AI can write the buying spreadsheet, at least until 2034.
fieldNote: Five years gives her a **specific idea**, dental nursing, from her aunt.
She still expects to **lose the buying job** and feels it keenly.
Saving means skipping **family events**, which costs her more than money.

steps.text: Look into the college dental nurse course done on the job
Save a hundred a month from Fridays and the gym
Stay at Clearway for as long as the buying job lasts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough for the country to sort something out, so they'd better. At work I'd say, let's not panic. I'd probably keep quiet with friends, because it would still feel far away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd probably wait too long. Ten years sounds like forever and I'm not someone who jumps. My buying job still goes, just later, and I'd be thirty-seven. I'd want to be trained in something hands-on by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at Clearway and see how things go for a couple of years. I'd start the dental nurse course maybe in year three, once I had some money saved. And I'd keep the spreadsheet going, because it still works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer, though I know calm is how I'd end up doing nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait. What would tell you it's time to move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Clearway brought in an AI system and Darren started using it, that'd be my sign. Or if they stopped hiring when people left. I'd notice that, because I'd be doing the extra work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your younger brother about all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He's nineteen and doing an accounting course, and I'd tell my brother to learn a trade alongside the accounting, because accounting is exactly what AI eats first. He'd roll his eyes. But I'd say it.

At work I'd say, **let's not panic**.
think: I'd probably **wait too long**, because I'm not someone who jumps.

fieldNote: The long runway invites her habit of **waiting**, and she says so herself.

steps.text: Wait two years and watch for an AI system at Clearway

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I wouldn't have time to do anything except move home. What would help is someone telling me straight which jobs will still exist, and a course I could do while still earning. Even a bit of money while retraining would make the difference.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what we'd lose. Nobody else at my firm knows that the cheap glove supplier tears in cold weather. That's the kind of thing I know from years of phone calls.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you. That's everything I wanted to ask.

headlineQuote: Nobody else at my firm knows that the cheap glove supplier tears in cold weather.
portrait: Aisha is a 27-year-old **cleaning supplies buyer** at a distributor that just lost its biggest contract.
She rents a room with a friend, has about **three weeks** saved and has never used AI tools.
She's already **anxious** in the plateau, because her firm is struggling regardless of AI.
Short warning leaves her **panicked**; longer warning gives her a dental nursing idea she may delay.
She values knowledge from **years of phone calls** that she fears no one will miss.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her only move would be going back to her parents'.
whatWouldHelp: Clear advice on **which jobs** will still exist.
A course she can do **while earning**, with some money while retraining.
